name: The China Brain
statement: If a billion people each played the part of one neuron, the whole nation would replicate a brain, yet surely feel nothing.
statementAccent: the whole nation would replicate a brain, yet surely feel nothing
meaning: The China brain, also called the Chinese Nation, is a thought experiment in the philosophy of mind devised by the philosopher Ned Block in his 1978 paper Troubles with Functionalism to argue against functionalism. Block asks you to imagine the entire population of China, about a billion people, organised to simulate the functional organisation of a single human brain: each person plays the role of one neuron, communicating with others by special two-way radios according to the same rules by which neurons signal one another, so that the whole population reproduces the exact causal organisation of someone's brain, complete with sensory inputs and behavioural outputs. Functionalism holds that mental states are defined by their functional roles, so any system with the right organisation should have the same mental states, including consciousness. Block finds it deeply counterintuitive that a nation of people passing signals would collectively feel pain or see colour, and uses this to argue that functionalism leaves out phenomenal consciousness, the absent qualia objection.
mechanism: The argument is a reductio aimed at functionalism's claim that the right functional organisation suffices for mind. Grant that the population of China can be arranged to instantiate exactly the functional organisation of a human brain, with each person acting as a neuron and the radio links standing in for synaptic connections; China is chosen because its population roughly matches the number of neurons in a brain. By functionalism, this system, being functionally identical to a conscious brain, would have the very same mental states, including qualitative experiences such as pain or the sight of red. Block contends that this is prima facie absurd: it seems the nation-system would have no inner experience at all, no felt quality to its states, even if it produced all the right outputs. If so, then a system can be functionally equivalent to a conscious being yet lack qualia, which means functional role does not capture phenomenal consciousness. The case is an intuition pump, and functionalists reply that the intuition is unreliable and that, arranged correctly, the system really would be conscious.

examples.text: Each of a billion people mimics one neuron, signalling others by radio on the same rules, so the nation as a whole realises the functional organisation of a brain.
Block finds it absurd that such a nation would feel pain or see red, suggesting a system can be functionally like a mind yet have no conscious experience.
Daniel Dennett and others answer that the China brain would in fact be conscious, treating the contrary intuition as an unreliable reaction to an unfamiliar system.

variants.name: The absent qualia objection
variants.text: The general claim, which the China brain illustrates, that a system can duplicate the functional organisation of a conscious being while lacking any qualitative experience.

variants.name: The Chinese Gym
variants.text: A related Block scenario in which people acting out a program collectively realise a mind's functional states, pressing the same doubt about qualia.

whyItMatters: The China brain is a classic objection to functionalism and to the broader idea that the right causal organisation is sufficient for consciousness. By imagining a mind realised in an unlikely medium, a whole nation swapping radio signals, it isolates the worry that phenomenal experience, the felt quality of seeing or hurting, might not be captured by functional role alone, giving sharp form to the absent qualia problem. The thought experiment sits alongside Searle's Chinese Room, the philosophical zombie, and the inverted spectrum in the debate over whether physical or functional facts settle the facts about consciousness, and it engages the idea of multiple realizability, that minds could be built from many materials.

working.lead: Realise a brain in a nation
working.text: arrange a billion people so that each acts as one neuron, reproducing the exact functional organisation of a human brain.
note that functionalism implies this system, being functionally identical to a brain, would have the same mental states, including conscious experience.
weigh the strong intuition that the nation would nonetheless feel nothing, which suggests functional role does not capture phenomenal consciousness.

limits: The China brain is an intuition pump, and its conclusion rests on the contested intuition that the nation-system would lack consciousness; functionalists such as Daniel Dennett reject this, holding that a system with the right organisation would genuinely be conscious and that our reluctance to say so reflects the scenario's unfamiliarity rather than a real absence of qualia. The case targets the claim that functional role suffices for phenomenal experience, not functionalism about all mental states, and it does not by itself establish any positive theory of consciousness. Some also question whether the scenario is coherent in detail, given the timescales and coordination it would require. So it frames the absent qualia challenge to functionalism rather than refuting the view, and how much force it carries depends on how far the guiding intuition is trusted.
misreadings: The China brain is not an argument that groups of people literally cannot think, but a challenge to the specific claim that duplicating a brain's functional organisation guarantees conscious experience. Its conclusion is a contested intuition, not a proven fact, since functionalists deny the system would lack qualia. And it concerns phenomenal consciousness, the felt quality of experience, not intelligent behaviour, so pointing out that the system could produce the right outputs does not answer Block's worry, which is precisely whether such outputs could occur with no inner experience at all.
origin: Devised by the philosopher Ned Block in his 1978 paper Troubles with Functionalism as an objection to functionalism, imagining the population of China organised as a brain to argue that functional organisation does not guarantee phenomenal consciousness.
